chunks: Measuring solenoid speed. The question: How can you measure the speed of a solenoid?
A solenoid's moving part, the plunger, travels a few millimeters in a few milliseconds. You cannot use a spinning-speed sensor (tachometer) on it, because nothing spins.
Instead you time the plunger between two known points, or track its position and see how fast it changes, or read its motion from the coil's own current.
The coil trick works because a moving plunger generates a small voltage that opposes the supply.
Think of timing a sprinter with two cones and a stopwatch. Start the watch at the first cone, stop it at the second, and divide the distance by the time.
Two sensors along the stroke do the same job.
The analogy breaks in one place: the plunger speeds up all the way to the end stop, so the average speed over the whole stroke is far lower than its speed at impact.
With a constant 24 volts the current first rises like a normal RL circuit, then falls as the plunger accelerates and generates speed voltage, hits a minimum at the moment of arrival (19.
5 milliseconds), then climbs toward 2 amps with the higher closed-state inductance. Without the plunger moving (blocked plunger) the curve would just keep rising.
Plunger (armature): the moving iron part of the solenoid. Stroke: how far the plunger travels. Transit time: the time to cross the stroke or a set segment.
Motional EMF: the voltage the moving plunger generates in the coil. It grows with speed and opposes the supply.
Current dip: the dip in coil current during pull-in, caused by that voltage. The dip ends at arrival.
A plunger crosses a 10 mm stroke in 8 milliseconds. Its average speed is 0. 010 over 0. 008 equals 1. 25 m/s. Now put two gates 5 mm apart and read a 2.
5 milliseconds gap between them. The speed there is 0. 005 over 0. 0025 equals 2 m/s. With no added sensor at all, drive the coil with a steady voltage and watch the current.
It rises, dips while the plunger moves fast, and climbs again once the plunger stops. That is the whole idea.
"I'd time the plunger between two known points: optical or Hall gates a set distance apart, velocity equals distance over time, with a hardware timer.
Or I differentiate a position sensor like a linear Hall or LVDT, with filtering.
Without a sensor, the coil gives velocity through the motional back-EMF, i dL over dx v , which makes a dip in the current during the stroke.
Lab check with a high-speed camera or laser."
